utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Would the registrar please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Milan Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Examination-in-chief by the Prosecutor still continuing. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Thank you, Your Honours. Before I continue with the examination-in-chief, the sequence of events that we were dealing with yesterday, there is one evidential matter that I want to raise. On the list of exhibits provided to the Chamber for the pre-trial proceedings, there was a list of documents and various other items that I indicated were not to be produced in evidence, and you can see them on the 65 ter list of exhibits. This afternoon my colleague Ms. Reidy discussed one of those exhibits with me; in particular, this witness' memoirs. And they're on the -- for the purposes of Defence counsel and for the Chamber, they can be found as B10 on the list of exhibits. I now take the view that those memoirs are relevant and would be of assistance to the Tribunal, and in effect, I want to change my mind about what I've written in the list, and so I intend to produce those to this witness and seek to tender them into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So you would like the witness to discuss them? MR. DI FAZIO: No. I just want him to identify him them, say they're his, and put them in. Anything that we need, as far as the Prosecution is concerned, at least, that we need, we can simply get from the written word, from the document itself. So I don't need to dwell on this particular piece of evidence. I simply want to tender it. I've taken the liberty of advising my colleagues from the Defence table that I propose to do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Okay. We have English translations? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Now, the haste of my decision, unfortunately, means that I don't have many -- or don't have sufficient copies. But as I said, I don't intend to dwell on them. I simply will ask the witness to identify them and then produce them into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. But we still need the English translations -- MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: -- for purposes of the record and for purposes of writing the judgement as well. MR. DI FAZIO: Oh, yes. There's no question about that. They won't simply be in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Are you tendering the English translation at a later stage? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. I'm told that we can provide the translation possibly this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Okay. So you notified the Defence counsels today? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, just a matter of moments ago. So it's the memoirs of Mr. Tihic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Written by himself. MR. DI FAZIO: Written by himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Okay. I'll hear from the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Madam President, Your Honours, we strongly object to this proposal from our learned colleague from the Prosecution on the basis that we act here according to the rules. We have very precise and stringent rules. Our colleagues from the Prosecution filed a list of exhibits, and therefore notified Defence about the list, exact list of the exhibits, and to some extent they gave us information about, I would say, evidence framework for this proceedings. It is a matter of principle; and due to that fact, I think if this application would be granted, then we are entering into an area of legal insecurity, because we have very precise rules. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Let me ask some questions, Counsel. You did receive these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Madam President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It was in pre-trial phase, during the process of reciprocal discovery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So you received them, and then, later on, that's when the Prosecution indicated that they were not going to use them in their case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That's right. And that was in -- I do believe it was in the month of April or something. So after this final approach, we obviously made our strategies towards the certain direction of list of exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Mr. di Fazio, I have a question of you. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: These memoirs, can you tell us if these notes -- I don't know what they are, maybe they are notes -- were they kept contemporaneously? Is this a contemporaneous document? MR. DI FAZIO: No. No, it's not a contemporaneous document. It's literally memoirs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Can you tell us when they were written and the basis of which you seek to admit these documents? MR. DI FAZIO: Would Your Honours just bear with me? The document itself, at least the English translation that I have, is undated, but I'm informed by my colleague that it was prepared -- the memoirs were prepared in April of 1995. The basis of admission of the document is that it is simply relevant. It is his memoirs of the period of time that we are dealing with. It is an account of the period of time that -- that we are dealing with, and therefore, on that basis alone, it immediately becomes relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: But what is the law on it? I can understand if he keeps a diary of a contemporaneous nature, it's admissible, in all probability. But if the document is kept much later, on what basis is it allowed? You should be able to go to some law on that now. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. I'm not aware of any particular decision that prohibits the admission of documentary evidence prepared at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: No. No. My question is what is the law that allows it, not prohibits it, because you're speaking in negative tones now. MR. DI FAZIO: Rule 89(C): "A Chamber may admit any relevant evidence which it deems to have probative value." That's Rule 89(C).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: You're aware of other rules as well. MR. DI FAZIO: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: The basic rule is, as far as documents are concerned in respect of being brought into evidence, they should be of contemporaneous nature.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Either kept on the day of the events or probably kept the next day or the day after, you see. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honour pleases, the rule or principle that you have just referred to is one with which I am immediately familiar and one which is completely apparent to me from having practised in Hong Kong and Australia, and I expect that it's a principle of law well known in common law jurisdictions with the rules of -- developed rules of evidence that they have in those domestic jurisdictions. My position is that there would be no such constriction upon this Chamber for the admission of the evidence; there would be no requirement of contemporaneity for the admission of the document. And so, in the absence of that rule, in the absence of any such rule, developed common law rules relating to the notions of contemporaneousness, you immediately have to go to first principles, and that's relevance. And if you look at it from that point of view, then I say that the memoirs must of necessity be relevant, because they deal with the events in 1992. And that would be my position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: But then again, on the first principles, you cannot subordinate admissibility to relevance. In the first place, you must have the right to produce it. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: But the other question I'd like to ask you, though, is that -- I mean, if there is any material in there which you would like to use, why not put it to him without looking at the diary and if he's able to say so -- because you have already been examining him now for, what, almost a week? MR. DI FAZIO: Oh, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Perhaps that might be a better course. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, yes, that would be one way of dealing with the issue. But they are, of course, lengthy memoirs, and they are, of course, detailed memoirs, and I'd -- it's a question of also time and expediency. I don't want to spend too much time getting too much detail. On the other hand, I don't suggest for one moment that the sort of detail contained in the memoirs would be unhelpful or is extraneous or simply would tax the Chamber. So that's the basis on which I can -- only basis on which I can seek to produce it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: But you see, at the same time, if you produce his memoirs -- and these memoirs, I don't know what length they are -- MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: You would be imposing on the Court quite unnecessary material as well. It is true that you may draw our attention to a couple of paragraphs. But if that's so, then I think you can put these questions to the witness, if you have already not put this evidence in. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Well, if that's the view of the Chamber, then so be it, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Because following up on the questions you've been answering, the rule is that where the witness is available, get the evidence from the witness viva voce. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And that would not put a strain on anybody, not even the Defence. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. I'm certainly not arguing against that principle, and I entirely agree that as a basic principle, that is the correct way to proceed. Evidence should normally go in by way of viva voce.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would counsel slow down, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We should apologise to the interpreters. We forget about them. MR. DI FAZIO: I should extend my apologies. I have no quarrel with the issue -- with the principle that the first source of evidence is viva voce evidence. I can really only seek to introduce this evidence by way of reference to two -- to the principle of relevance and on the basis that it will, I say, I submit, assist the Chamber by the provision of even greater detail. But that's the highest that I can put it at. And I don't -- I've nothing more to put to the Chamber in terms of its eligibility for admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: May I have a word?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Did you want to say anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just a few seconds, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I would kindly and friendly remind my colleagues from the Prosecution that we have here a case law regarding that issue; namely it is the Krstic case with regard to the admission of evidence during the course of the trial, as well as Prijedor case and Krnojelac Foca prison case. So we have plenty of case law with regard to that issue. And needless to emphasise, that we are not feeling secure in the course these proceedings if we shall be in situation to be faced with numerous evidences which might be out of blue came to our attention at that particular day. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will make the decision after the break. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Can the witness be shown the bundle of photographs. There's just four more photographs that I want to show him. Exhibit P14, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, I just want you to look at photograph F18, and if you may at the same time also look at photograph F19, please. Both photographs appear to depict vacant land with grass growing. Firstly, can you tell us where the location of those photographs is?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is in Bosanski Samac, in an area where the mosque used to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Where was the mosque?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was here, in a park.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We need the use of the ELMO, Mr. di Fazio, so that the accused persons can follow the proceedings, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Just point out where the structure of the mosque was on photograph F18, please.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was somewhere around here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And just for the sake of completeness, indicate it on F19, please.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you would now look at photographs F40 and F41. We can see a structure there, and what is that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This building is the Orthodox church.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. In the area -- the vacant area depicted in the photograph immediately in front of the Orthodox church in F40, was it always vacant land?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is where the Catholic church used to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you would just quickly look at F41. Is it the case that on the left you can see the Orthodox church?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that is the Orthodox church.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And so if I understand your evidence correctly, the Catholic church stood across the road, and you can see the vacant area on the right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, across the road from the Catholic church. You could see that on the previous photograph. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. I've finished with the photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yesterday, Mr. Tihic, we had arrived at the point where you were taken to Batajnica, and you described some of the activities, for want of a better word, that occurred there. How long did you remain at Batajnica?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 3rd until the 27th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What about Dragan Lukac?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragan Lukac was there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were those two men that I've mentioned ever taken away from Batajnica while you still were there?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I have already mentioned that Fadil Topcagic and another person came from Bosanski Samac and that they took [redacted], Dragan Lukac, Franjo Barugdzic [phoen], and another person from the area of the municipality of Modrica or Gradacac to be exchanged. I don't know where is it that they actually took them, but I do know that they took them away from that room, and later on I learned that they were in fact taken to Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll get on to that episode shortly, but I'm really referring to before that. Were [redacted] or Dragan Lukac and possibly other men ever taken away for a short period of time?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the early days, in the first few days that we spent in Batajnica, soldiers came, ordered them to take off the clothes they had, gave them some military clothes, and they -- a couple of them, including Selmo Mujkanovic, they put on those military clothes and were taken outside of that area. Later on I learned that they were in the Zemun prison. They came back a couple of days later. Zemun is part of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Is Zemun in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's quite close to Batajnica, 20 or 30 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The ethnic background of the prisoners in Batajnica, can you comment upon that, please?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were Bosniaks, Croats, and there was an American who was brought in later.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What was his name?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember now, but I know that he used to tell us that he was married to a Croat woman and he had joined the Croatian army and was captured in Brcko. I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You've described mistreatment that occurred at Batajnica: being forced to sing songs and being humiliated by being forced to engage in bizarre exercises and beatings. Other than that, was there any other sort of mistreatment that you observed?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were also interrogations. They would take us one by one to a building where we were interrogated. And on one occasion we were taken to a TV show. We were to be taped, and we were supposed to say something, and I think that one of the police officers hit me on that occasion because I was saying things that were, in his view, untrue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What about the American? Did you ever see him mistreated?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They beat him. It was quite interesting, in fact. He would not moan at all for a while, until a lieutenant came, and he held his hands like this. This was some kind of a yoga exercise. And when they separated his hands like this, then he started to moan too. Right at the very end, he wore a collar around his neck because they hurt his neck in some way, his spine, and later on I saw him at Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was beating the only form of mistreatment suffered by the American?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, in the same way as they maltreated us, they would us ask us, "How large is Serbia?" And then we would have to say, "It reaches all the way to Tokyo." He also had to sing songs, and all those soldiers were really maltreating us in various ways. They forced him to say things against America, just as they forced us to say things, but they did have it in for him particularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you know a gentleman named Zdravko Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They brought the two of them together. According to what they told us, they went from Zupanija to Brcko, and they were captured there by the JNA as they ate a meal of cevapcici, and then they were brought to Batajnica. And then Zdravko was together with me in Sremska Mitrovica, in the camp there. They beat Zdravko quite badly too. He was in his 20s. The lad was in his 20s.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was Zdravko Filipovic incarcerated at Batajnica at the same time as the American?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were brought in together at the same time, and they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was Zdravko Filipovic mistreated in any way apart from beatings?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was also maltreated, as was everybody else. The two of them were beaten more than the rest of us because they had already had their way with us, so to speak, and they were new. This guy was an American, he was in the Croatian army, and that's why they singled him out for special abuse. They beat them really bad. They used brass knuckles on their backs, and they kicked them in the kidneys.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In the time that you were at Batajnica, did you see any sexual mistreatment of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They forced the American and Zdravko to take off their underpants and to simulate intercourse.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Is this in front of other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It happened that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were you photographed at all in the time that you were at Batajnica? I just mean photographed. Not interviewed, photographed.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One day, they came and they gave us a disposable razor, just one, to shave. We had quite long beards at the time because we couldn't shave at all, so it was quite hard to shave, but we managed somehow. Then they took us to a park, myself, Izet, Lukac - Dragan Lukac - [redacted]. [redacted]. There were perhaps five, six, up to ten journalists who took photographs of us. And then they took us back. The next day -- I'm sorry. The next day, I know that the soldiers came with some newspapers where it was described how we had slaughtered Serbian children and then they beat us, especially hard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you -- [inaudible]?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's the way they were telling us. They were showing us the newspaper with our pictures in the newspapers, and the reservists came. They did not -- they had no idea that we were criminals of this sort. And then they beat us, despite the fact that the journalists never interviewed us at all. They told me that allegedly the Muslim side had sentenced me to death, but I did not see that. That's what they told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Apart from photographs, were you ever interviewed whilst at Batajnica?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A TV team came and made a TV programme about us. I know that it was broadcast. We were also cast in a negative light. And the next day after that programme, we were beaten again. They placed us in a context of the events in Bosanski Brod where allegedly somebody had slaughtered Serbian children and raped the women. I concluded this on the basis of what the people who were beating us were saying. They were saying, "You were doing this and that," despite the fact that we had nothing to do with it. And there was -- there were interrogations. A major from the state security service wanted to talk to us. The conversation was actually quite all right. It lasted for about two hours, and we discussed political issues in general. No record was made, and I was not made to sign anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Just briefly explain to the Chamber how it was that in the course of the TV programme that was made about you, they were able to place you in a context of events at Bosanski Brod. How was this achieved?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One day, maybe seven or eight days after our arrival, they brought in some people from various places, one of them, Aljo, who was killed, who died of the beating, was from -- he was from Sijelcovac, near Bosanski Brod. There was a little lieutenant from Tuzla, some Croats from villages around Modrica. And that was probably -- they say that Alija was also in this TV programme. That may have been the way in which they placed us in this context. They can edit things. I did not see this programme, but according to the response of the reactions of the guards, I got the impression that I was also labelled a slaughterer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you eventually transferred from Batajnica?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 27th of May, we were transferred to Sremska Mitrovica. That was a military camp, military prisoner camp. It was in the former prison building. This building was constructed in Austro-Hungarian times.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was this actually a proper prison in the sense of a building constructed for that purpose?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a large complex. It was a well-known prison in the former Yugoslavia. And perhaps one fourth of this complex was used as the military prison camp. There were prisoners from Vukovar and 13 people from Bosnia. There may have been some other people too, but I know about the 13 people from Bosnia who were transferred there from Batajnica. These are large buildings, old buildings, with a big four-metre tall wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Is Sremska Mitrovica in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Sremska Mitrovica is in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was any reason given to you as to why you were being transferred from Batajnica to Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They didn't tell us anything. They simply told us to get ready. They handcuffed us. Some new military police officers came, put us into Pinzgaver vehicles, and took us to Mitrovica. At that time, we did not know where we were going. In fact, one of the guards did tell us that we were going to Sremska Mitrovica; Ivica Pavisic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were you accompanied by anyone who -- anyone from Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Just the police, military police officers. They sat in the back with us. And as soon as we lifted our heads, we would be hit with a truncheon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I think you mentioned earlier in your evidence a gentleman named Selmo Mujkanovic. Who was that person?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Selmo Mujkanovic was with me in all the camps. We were in fact handcuffed together with the steel cuffs, because they handcuffed us in pairs and put us into Pinzgavers that way. He was a police officer. He used to be a police officer in the Bosanski Samac police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What I want to know is did he -- did he accompany you to Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We were handcuffed together in the Pinzgaver vehicle, and we actually shared a room.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Describe for the Chamber your accommodation, the living circumstances that you experienced at Sremska Mitrovica, please.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Sremska Mitrovica, we were in a big room, perhaps 25 metres long and seven, eight metres wide. There were 50 of us there, 52, 53, thereabouts. We were from Bosnia, and the rest of the people were all from Vukovar. At the bottom of the room was a sink where we could wash and the toilet. We were again beaten, mistreated. When we arrived, this is where it was -- when it was especially dangerous because we were beaten -- stripped naked and beaten until 2.00 or 3.00 in the morning. When you faint, they take you back to the cell, and when you come to, they take you out again. One of them told me to lie down on the desk, and he beat me on the -- on my abdomen. I told him not to do that because I had surgery, and he asked me where I had the surgery. I showed him the scar, and then he beat me on the scar. This was really terrible, this beating. It lasted until 6.00 in the morning. There was a captain who was a Croat. He remained in the JNA despite that fact. And then he stopped the beating. But later on, they again beat us. In Mitrovica, they beat us according to a schedule. After the breakfast and after the evening, that was the collective beating. And then in the meantime, they would take out whoever they fancied and beat that person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, how long before did you have your surgery? How long before did you have your surgery? How many years before? How long earlier?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1972. That's where I -- when I had my surgery. And now we are talking about 1992. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What was the surgery for?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had an ileus, and that's why they had to cut out one metre of my intestines. I also had a surgery on my left hip, and I asked him not to hit me on the leg, on the hip, and he intentionally beat me precisely on those places where it hurt the most. In the morning, I was unable to sit up because my whole body hurt, and this Pavisic brought in a doctor, a lady doctor. They told me to strip, and then he asked me, "Who beat you?" And I said, "Nobody did," because the guy who beat me stood right next to him. Then he asked me what I was by profession. I said I was a lawyer. And he said, "Shame on you. You're a lawyer and you're lying." But the other guys who said who beat them, as soon as Pavisic left, they were beaten again. The lady doctor could not believe my blood pressure. She took my blood pressure, and she was unable to believe the reading. She had to take it several times to make sure that it was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was there any singing of patriotic songs?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the same as in all the other camps. We had the standard songs. Let me call them Chetnik songs.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for His Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Did you suffer from low blood pressure or high blood pressure at that time?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Low, low blood pressure. I always had low pressure. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. In the time that you were at Sremska Mitrovica, were you interviewed?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Just before we were exchanged, the camp commander came, around 6.00 a.m., and he called out a man by the name of Filip Karaula, a German by the name of Kurt [phoen], and myself. We went out. Two police officers with electric batons were with him. We thought that we had been called out to be beaten. We were facing the wall. And then he said -- he couldn't pronounce "R" correctly, and there was a team of foreign journalists. He said, "I want you to give a statement to him. I want you to say that nobody beat you, that you have proper hygienic conditions, that you are entitled to walk, to have a walk, in accordance with the regulations of the Red Cross." He asked us, "Is that clear?" We said, "Yes." He said, "Do you have any questions?" And I said, "If they ask me what happened before in Samac regarding the Arkan's men and so on ..." He said, "I'm not interested in that, but you'll be better off not talking, because they can always come here and take their revenge." Then they took us to have a haircut and to wash. Then we gathered up all the nicest clothes we had, and we put them on. They took us to give an interview. This man nicknamed Plavisa [phoen], who was the chief security officer, was present there. There was also the camp commander. We gave a statement, and it was broadcast. They wanted me to denounce -- actually, to call upon Alija Izetbegovic to exchange the JNA soldiers that had been captured in Bosnia for us, and that's what I did. I called upon him to do that. They told me then, "Tihic, it is up to you and your statement whether you will be exchanged or not." That's what the commander told me. There had been this rumour going on about this big exchange that would take place, and this was, in fact, the exchange in which I also was exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Who were the interviewers? Where were they from?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I understood later, it was Sky News, and the journalist was their correspondent from Serbia. He spoke our language. So that is what I gathered. I know that he had a beard. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. I'd like to show the Chamber a short video and indeed ask the witness to identify this short video. I understand it's been provided to the technical people, and we have transcripts of the video in English and in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The title of the video, please. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, it's referred to in -- I think the best way, so that we can easily identify it at a later time, would be "Sulejman Tihic interview in Sremska Mitrovica." Perhaps before it's shown, Mr. Tihic, can I ask you to pay attention to the video that will be shown now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Before it is shown, can we have the scripts. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, and for the benefit of those in the technical box, I really propose to do what I did on the last occasion and just get Mr. Tihic to identify the occasion, unless there's objections from the Chamber and from the Defence. It's only a short video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We shall have the numbers first. So can we have the number, the video and the transcripts, both the English and the Serbo-Croat.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The video of the interview with Sulejman Tihic shall be marked for the record Prosecution Exhibit P17, and the transcript shall be marked for the record as Prosecution's Exhibit P17A, and the B/C/S version shall be P17A ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. The Prosecution can proceed. MR. DI FAZIO: If perhaps it now can be played.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, can you identify the occasion that's depicted in that videotape, at least insofar as you appear in it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in Sremska Mitrovica, as it was said here, a few days before the exchange, and these are the rooms, the premises, of the camp in Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. You foreshadowed a question of mine. You had an opportunity to see the buildings and the men marching around depicted in the video?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a common thing, a common position there. You had to crouch, put your head between your knees. When you went out, you had to keep your head down. When you talked to some officials, you again had to keep your head down.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. One of the persons who spoke in the course of the interview was apparently a gentleman named Filip Karaula. Do you know that person?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Filip was in the same room with me. As he told us, he was the commander of a part of the defence in Vukovar, of a part which is called Mitnica, and I guess when those others fled, he just stayed behind as the leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. You saw your appearance, the way you looked in the video, at least the upper part of your body, and the Chamber has heard your evidence regarding the beatings and the mistreatment that you suffered in all of these prisoners but also Sremska Mitrovica. So I ask you the same question that I did the other day: How can you reconcile, or how do you reconcile your appearance with the evidence that you've given of beatings and so on?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave this statement two or three days before the exchange. About seven days before the exchange, the order had arrived not to beat us anymore, so that we could look more or less decent at the time of the exchange, because there would be the Red Cross present and others. So that that was one of the reasons. And it is also due to the fact that this Simo, who beat most, one day suddenly turned up and called out me and Kedacic and - I don't know - Mujkanovic, and we thought he would call us out so as to beat us. But he said to lift our heads, because we kept them down. And he said, "Lift your heads," so we did, and looked at him. And he said, "I apologise to all of you. I'm sorry that I beat you." This was incredible. We couldn't believe our ears, because Simo instilled terrible fear in all of us. And then he said, "We had been informed from Batajnica that you had slaughtered some Serb children, and that was why I beat you." So that for about 15 or 20 days, as soon as we had been amnestied, to put it that way, by Simo, then we began to recover a little then about seven days prior to the exchange, total prohibition to beat us arrived. I mean, that was violated too, but there was no further beating in the true sense of the word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. di Fazio, I wonder whether I can ask

utterances.speaker: MR. TIHIC
utterances.text: What was the surname of the man Simo you're referring to here, please?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know his last name. I know he was Simo. I know he was a big man. There was something in his eyes which seemed to show that he wasn't quite normal, and if -- and I know because he talked to our doctor, to Miroslav Kedacic and complained to him that he -- some problem, that he had headaches, that he had some other complaints. And he only told us that his name was Simo. He never gave us his full name. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I think -- I'm sure Your Honour will correct me if I'm wrong, but this Simo has got nothing to do with the defendant in our case, Mr. Simo Zaric?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he doesn't. No, no, he doesn't. No. It was a soldier, and guarded us there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you ever work whilst you were held at Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One day they called us all out, the whole camp, and lined us up along the building, hands behind our backs, heads down, and we didn't know where they were taking us. Then some vehicles arrived, some vans, I think furniture vans, no windows or anything, and they loaded us onto those vans. It was August, so it was very hot. And they forced more people into a van than we could properly fit, and then when we'd be all up there, they would run up to us with their batons and push us so as to fit -- to squeeze more people in. It was very stuffy because these vans were closed from all sides. There was no air to breathe. And then we -- they would take us somewhere for about -- the ride lasted half an hour, perhaps, and then we fetched up on a rather large plot of land, in a meadow, and then they again lined us up. The length of a line was about 400 or 500 metres, and we were all lined up like that, and we faced that field or something. It was a sugar beet field. And of course all kinds of thoughts then occurred to you, "Will they kill me here or what?" But now we were ordered to weed out that field of sugar beet, and that's what we did that whole day. There was a lunch break, and they brought us something to eat there. And then they took us back in the evening. Otherwise, the routine was to clean the rooms, to clean the command offices, the corridors, the WCs, and the like. Quite often, I volunteered to do that because it was better than to just sit in a cell and wait for them to come and take you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were you eventually exchanged?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The big exchanges that took place between Yugoslavia and Croatia, and we Bosnians were included in that. It was on the 14th of August at Nemetin, near Osijek. It was also a painstaking exchange. It took from 3.00 in the morning until 8.00 -- 1800. We drove through all the Vojvodina villages. People would board the vehicles, hit us, kick us, spit on us, call us Ustasha, but, well, an end came to that too. There were 15 buses, you know, and I think that in every village we would stop and the crowd would board the buses, ask questions, hit, kick, swear at you. Then they'd give some brandy to the policemen, and the policemen drink and, of course, intoxicated, start to give even more vent to that. Another one -- one of the -- one of them said, "Look, we tried to make them look nice for the exchange and now, you fool, look what you're doing to them." And the major says, "Well, because they were swearing at my mother," which of course does not stand to reason. And as the first man gets off the bus, the policeman just hits him and then the major tells him, "Now, I'll swear at your mother," and so on and so forth. So that this exchange also was very painstaking and painful.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Where was -- what was the location of the actual exchange? Was it in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was in Croatia. That's what that place is called, Nemetin, near Osijek.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What did you do once you arrived in Croatia? I don't want you to take us step by step through this. I just want you to tell the Chamber how you handled your freedom in Croatia, what were the main things you did after your release. For instance, did you get medical treatment?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When the exchange was over, I was met by my family members. They took me to Rijeka. All those who were in the camp went to have medical checkups. We were also allowed -- granted some summer holidays somewhere on the coast for three weeks. I used only one week of that. And I went for a medical checkup. It turned out that I had some broken ribs which had healed in the meantime. But the sternal bone had already -- had already cracked, and also this bone here, and my front teeth were also broken. But I managed to put that more or less right. After I came out of the camp, I couldn't sleep for about a month because one simply didn't know, "Am I in the camp? What is the truth and what is a dream?" But gradually, it fades, it fades out, it fades away, and now I feel well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you eventually make your way back to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: When did you get back to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between 1994 and 1996, I was in Germany, worked for the Bosnian embassy. And then in 1996, I returned to Sarajevo. And from 1996, I've been living in Sarajevo; September 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What did you do in the Bosnian embassy in Germany?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since I am a lawyer, I was the head of the consular department, dealing with the issue of passports and various documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you now live in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes, in Sarajevo. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, if Your Honours please, I think I've just about come to the end of my examination-in-chief. If you propose to take a break this afternoon, would now be a suitable time to do so? I only ask that because, if possible, I'd like an opportunity just to confer with my colleagues over the examination-in-chief and see if there is anything that I've missed. But I can indicate that even if I have missed something, it would only be a matter of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Just one question here. You're now back in Sarajevo. What do you do there now?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am in Sarajevo now, and I work professionally as the Vice-President of the Party for Democratic Action. That is the largest party in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I'm also the Vice-President of the People's Assembly of Republika Srpska, which is one of the two entities in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We have no problem. I think we can take our -- in which case, we will have a longer break because we are supposed to resume at 1615 hours. MR. DI FAZIO: If indeed, as I expect, this is the end of my examination-in-chief, the issue of how we proceed later in the afternoon might arise. Shall we deal with that then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: At 1615? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We will have our break, and we will resume at 1615, quarter past 4.00. --- Break taken at 3.40 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will give its decision on the motion by -- on the application by the Prosecution to reinstate the memoirs of the witness on the exhibit list and to have them admitted, to which the Defence objected and gave their reasons. The Trial Chamber did put questions to the Prosecution which were answered. The Trial Chamber is of the view that since the witness is available, he should have been able to give evidence of any material facts in the memoirs, besides the fact that the notes were not made contemporaneously, that is, as the events happened. We were informed that they were made in 1995. That is quite some time after the events. We do not see why the Prosecution -- we were not informed, rather, why the Prosecution changed their mind at the time that -- during the pre-trial stage, and it is indeed in keeping with the Rules of Procedure and Evidence that the case for the Prosecution, including the evidence that they intended to produce at trial, is laid on the table before the trial starts. In the event of new evidence, of course, being available, the Trial Chamber would take the interests of justice into account, besides any other considerations, to decide the issue. In the instant case, the memoirs have been available with the Prosecution for some time. It appears to have been a case of lack of diligence on the part of the Prosecution. The objection by the Defence is therefore sustained. The witness is still on the stand. Any other matters by the Prosecution in examination-in-chief? MR. DI FAZIO: No. I've finished my examination-in-chief, thank you, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I would like to turn to the Defence and find out how many Defence counsel intend to cross-examine this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, as far as I'm concerned, I'm going to have at least a maximum 15 minutes of cross-examination, and I understand that the all counsels would like to pose some questions in cross. And we have decided that we shall start with Mr. Pisarevic as a starter for the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pisarevic, how long do you think you will take, just roughly?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, to be honest, Your Honours, perhaps an hour, an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And then the other counsel, of course. That will mean more than the time that we have today. Yes, you may sit down, counsel. You may sit down. Perhaps we can go into private session to discuss the arrangements further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: There is just one matter that I want to raise with the Chamber, if I may, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, please. MR. DI FAZIO: It's just a question of, I'll be frank, convenience to the Prosecution. If I call this witness -- when we call this witness, that effectively ends my ability to speak to him and proof him, continue to proof him. Would it be amenable to the Defence and to the Trial Chamber if I used the time available to us to simply lead him through personal matters and background material and not get on to the actual events of incarceration or any of the events that formed the basis of material in the indictment and still be permitted to speak to him? Because we've got tomorrow off and the weekend and so on before he continues. And if the Chamber is amenable to that, would you be prepared to waive the rule that I should not speak to witnesses once they've started to give their evidence? That's the only matter that I wanted to raise. I don't know if the Defence have any attitude towards that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Maybe I can hear from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I do believe it's perfectly fine with us. I mean, within limits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You have no problem with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No. I think I'm speaking on behalf of all my colleagues. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Prosecution will be allowed to speak to the witness tomorrow -- before Monday, that is, okay. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And the other question you asked, whether you would be permitted to lead him on the matters which are not in contention, yes, you can go ahead, as long as you limit it to matters which are particulars and facts which are not in contention. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. What I proposed to deal with mainly was background material and go as far as I could with that until I get to what I think is probably going to be contentious material and then stop my examination-in-chief at that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Of course the Defence will be following, and if they feel it's leading on a contentious matter, then they will say so. There are no protective measures for the coming witness? MR. DI FAZIO: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So we will remain in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Will the witness please make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you, please sit down. The Prosecution, please. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Your full name is Dragan Lukac?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: When were you born?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: 16th of October, 1956.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And are you a married man?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you have children?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: I do, two.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Where do you currently reside?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: In Orasje at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How would you describe your ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: I am of Croat ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What's your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: I teach philosophy and sociology.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Where do you do that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: At present, in Sarajevo at the Federal Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And how long have you been doing that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: Well, I've held the present job for the last five months -- for the last five months, but I've worked for the police for some 20 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Your current position in the Federal Ministry of the Interior, is that somehow attached to the police?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: At present, I'm acting director of the federal police under the Ministry of the Interior -- under the Federal Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And what sort of -- what exactly do your duties there in that position involve?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: It involves planning and supervision of all police operations within the Federal Ministry of the Interior of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in simplest terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I want to ask you some questions about your past, your background. Where were you raised?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: I grew up in a village near Bosanski Samac, and from 1989, I've lived in Bosanski Samac. I'm referring to the pre-war period. Excuse me, 1979.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. In the former Yugoslavia, was it compulsory to perform some sort of military service as a young man?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: It was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you perform any such military service?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And can you tell the Chamber what that was and when, when you actually performed that military service?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: I served in 1982, 1983. I did a year-long service, and I attended the reserve -- the school for reserve officers at Sremski Karlovci [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you acquire any rank while you were doing that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: I was lieutenant -- second lieutenant when I left the army and then lieutenant four years later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just a little intervention. I think the witness said "Karlovac" and not "Sremski Karlovac." It's different place. Karlovci is in Croatia. Karlovac, not Sremski Karlovac. It is line 16 page 38, 16, "School for reserve officers at Sremski Karlovci." So I think the precise place is Karlovac, Croatia. As I suggested before - pardon me, Madam President - I think for the most people out of former Yugoslavia, it should be wise to use when -- I mean, it's a suggestion for the Prosecution. When you are speaking with your witness and when the name of time -- town appears, it's not problem to say where it is, Croatia, Bosnia, Serbia, something like that, to be more familiar, if it's not a big problem, of course. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sure the Prosecutor will clarify that and will take note. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You heard that exchange. Can you just clarify the town where you did your military service, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: I served in Karlovac, in the then Socialist Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were you aware of a Territorial Defence system operating in the former Yugoslavia, a TO system as sometimes people refer to it? Just let us know if you were aware of it or not.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: You could say that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, reserve officer school, did it produce officers for the TO system?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Precisely for the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was that as opposed to the JNA? In contrast to the JNA, perhaps is a better way of putting it.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: Not in contrast with, because the armed forces of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia included two components. One of them was the active-duty forces. That was the JNA. And the other one was the Territorial Defence, which was, to all intents and purposes, the reserve force, which would then be engaged in case of a war in the territory of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In the time that you conducted your military service for that year, did you become acquainted with the structure of the JNA, the way it operated, the way it was set up in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: Well, we did acquire some knowledge about certain issues during our training.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What did you do following your completion of service in the reserve, army reserve?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: Before I went to do my military service, I worked for the Municipal Department for the Interior, in Bosanski Samac. And after my military service I returned back to my old job, to the old unit that I was with before I had left for my army service.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. So in effect, your military service interrupted your civilian career, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the position that you had acquired with the Municipal Department for the Interior?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: Before I went to do my military service, and after it, I was a CID inspector in the Municipal Secretariat for the Interior in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: For the sake of brevity, is the Municipal Secretariat for the Interior also known by the acronym as "the SUP"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: That's right. Except because at that time it was not called "the Ministry" but "the Secretariat of the Interior," and that was sekretariat za uno trasnje poslava [phoen]. So that SUP is the acronym for the Secretariat of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Following your reserve military training, you resumed your career as CID man, a CID inspector?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Where were you based?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: In Bosanski Samac. In the territory of the Bosanski Samac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you receive promotion at all?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: I kept that job, that office, until the 31st of December, 1986.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And what happened then?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: And from the 1st of January, 1987, I was appointed acting secretary of the Secretariat of the Interior of the municipality of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: That's quite a mouthful. Does that essentially mean that you were in the police?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: Yes. But it's not that I worked for the police only; I was the number one there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And what sort of work did that position entail?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: Well, that office presumes managing the whole police authority in the municipality of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How long did you keep that position?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: I stayed there until the 1st of July, 1987; that is, six months.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And following that, what position did you take up?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: After that I was appointed head of the public security in the same secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How long did you retain that position?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: And I kept that office, as far as I can remember, until November 1987.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Please continue. What career change occurred after November 1987?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: Then -- yes, there was a change, because the police in Bosnia-Herzegovina underwent a reorganisation at that time. It involved the abolition of municipal secretariats of the Interior and the establishment of public security stations in municipalities and incorporation of these stations in the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was -- which practically meant a higher level of centralisation of the police in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And were you appointed chief of the criminal division of that public security station?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: Yes, I was appointed chief of the CID department in that police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were you in charge of uniformed police officers, or some different aspect of police work?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: No, not the uniformed police; only the criminal investigation police.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What sort of area did you cover?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: All aspects of crime, of criminal activities in the territory of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. I was actually referring more to a geographical area. What sort of geographical area were you responsible for?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: This is the -- geographically, this is the territory of Bosanski Samac, which means 26 localities. Twenty-five are villages and one town; that is, that of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How long did you retain that position?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: I remained in that position until the 11th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What happened on the 11th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: On the 11th of April, 1992, the Republican Ministry of the Interior appointed me acting chief of the public security station in the Bosanski Samac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: May I just return briefly to your military service. After you completed your year with the army reserve, did you retain any reservist status?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: Yes. My assignment was duty within then Territorial Defence units for the territory of the Bosanski Samac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How long did you keep up that assignment, that duty?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: I kept it since I -- since my return from the military service, which was August or September 1983, until the 1st of January, 1987.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Why did it come to an end?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: I stopped doing that because I was appointed the acting secretary of the Secretariat of the Interior in the municipality, and according to the law, I had to be in charge of the police in case of any war-type situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to turn now to the TO, the TO system that existed in Yugoslavia. Can you explain to the Chamber precisely how it worked in the former Yugoslavia, how it was structured, what its main functions were?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: Well, I can't be very specific, but I can give you a rough overview of the structure of the Territorial Defence as it was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence in the former Yugoslavia was organised on the level of the republics, unlike the other component, the active-duty component, the JNA, which was organised on the level of the entire state. The structure of the Territorial Defence was organised at the republican level, where you had the republican TO staff. And below the republican staff, there were regional Territorial Defence staffs. I think there were nine such regions in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but I'm not quite sure about the number. And then at the level of municipalities, you had the municipal Territorial Defence staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber what, in practical terms, it actually meant to have a TO structure at the municipal level? Did they have an office? Did they have weapons? Did they have meetings? Did they have drills? Did they recruit? Tell the Chamber what it actually looked like to see the TO at work at the municipal level.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: Citizens able to serve in the military after their national service were assigned, in accordance with their ability, to the structures of the Territorial Defence units that were set up at the municipal level. Some citizens were also assigned to active units of the JNA as reservists, because that was their assignment. The Territorial Defence was composed of several units which had a certain purpose. I don't know how many such units were, for instance, in the municipality of Bosanski Samac. The TO staff, the commander of the staff, with a certain number of reserve officers working in the staff, was a standing organ which existed in Bosanski Samac, and this is where these people worked on a daily basis. They were employed there. And if there were some military exercises, some units were raised and then they underwent the training that was carried out during such exercises. They were called up. Such staffs had certain administrative personnel which provided services to the staff and enabled it to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did the TOs have weapons?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence had a certain quantity of weapons. It was stored in the depots of the Territorial Defence over a certain period of time. It was stored in the depots which existed in each municipality and also Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was there only one depot of weapons per municipality, or were weapons stored in various depots within a municipality?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: I don't know the situation in other municipalities, but as far as I know, in Bosanski Samac there was just one storage site. This is where the weapons were stored.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And what sort of weapons did the TO normally have? Were they light weapons, heavy weapons, artillery?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: I think that these were mostly infantry weapons, with a certain quantity of artillery pieces, with the appropriate quantities of ammunition for such weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I want to turn from the general structure of the TO to some questions about Bosanski Samac itself and the municipality. I think everyone agrees that there were three main ethnic groups living in the municipality: Croats, Serbs, and Muslims. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: There were, I think, a number of villages surrounding the town of Bosanski Samac. Were they divided into either Croat or Serb villages?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: I have already said that in the municipality of Bosanski Samac, there were 26 inhabited areas or localities. Twenty-five were villages and one was a town. As regards the ethnic composition of the population in the municipality of Bosanski Samac, I can say that in -- that Croats lived in a certain number of villages, Serbs lived in a number of villages, and there were villages where both Serbs and Croats lived, while Bosniaks in our municipality lived exclusively in the town of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Within the town of Bosanski Samac, did you find members of all three ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: Yes. Bosniaks, Croats, and Serbs, and others lived in the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did they confine themselves to particular areas of the town, or did they -- were they mixed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: They were mixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the term Posavina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Pre-April 1992, if someone had mentioned that word to you, what would it have meant to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: It would have meant a region within Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can you describe it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: It's an area located in the north eastern part of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It covered an area including several municipalities. In addition to Bosanski Samac, there was also the municipality of Derventa, the municipality of Bosanski Brod, the municipality of Odzak, of Modrica, of Orasje, of Brcko, a part of the Gradacac municipality, and a part of the Doboj municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do I take your answer to mean that those municipalities that you've just mentioned formed part of the Posavina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: These municipalities made up the region of Bosanska Posavina, Bosnian Posavina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Again, I think it's generally agreed that the Sava River, which flows close to Bosanski Samac, forms the border with Croatia. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In pre-April 1992, were there bridges crossing the Sava River into Croatia in the Posavina area, and if so, can you tell the Chamber how many bridges there were, where they were?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: There were bridges. I don't know how many bridges there were exactly, but there was a bridge between Bosanski and Slavonski Samac. There was another bridge connecting Bosanski and Slavonski Brod. There was another bridge connecting Orasje and Zupanja. There was another bridge connecting Brcko and Guna on the other bank of the river in Croatia. There was also a bridge connecting Bosanska Gradiska, and I don't know the place on the other bank of the river in Croatia. These would be the bridges in the vicinity of Bosanski Samac, relatively speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: May it be convenient for Trial Chamber to have a map and then witness can go to the map? I mean local map of Bosanski Samac and Posavina. It's just a suggestion, of course. I'm not pressing that issue. Sorry. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm about to leave the topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, I think the Prosecution will be left to present their case the way they see fit. MR. DI FAZIO: I was going to skim over this topic, and I've dealt with it. I don't feel that it's necessary at this stage, if Your Honours please, to make reference to any map. I may do so later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: I think this is the kind of information also perhaps if you have it at your fingertips you can even suggest to him, because I'm sure these are incontrovertible facts which can be found in any common tourist book if you -- MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: So I mean, subject of course to any objection that might be raised, that might make the proceedings go a little faster. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. I'm grateful to Your Honour for that suggestion, but as I said I intend to leave -- unless the Chamber wants me to re-go over this evidence and point out the areas on the map, I'm going to leave the topic of geography and move on to another matter. Thank you. I'm grateful to Your Honours for the suggestions made.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Just going back to your personal background, were you ever a member of the Communist Party in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of the League of Socialists of Yugoslavia until 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: When did you join?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were you a member of that -- of the League of Socialists as a result of genuine belief or heart-felt belief, genuine political commitment, or was there some other reason for your membership of that organisation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: I think this was not a political belief or ideological belief. In the political system as it was in the former Yugoslavia, it was a necessity, a requirement, if you wanted to prosper in your job. And if you wanted to get a job at all, you had to be a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you eventually -- sorry, you left in 1989. Did you join any other political party?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: No, I did not join any other political party. And I have not been a member of any political party ever since.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: There has been evidence in the case that there were democratic elections in 1990 and nationalist parties emerged. Does that sit well with your recollection of events?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, at the municipal elections, six political parties participated in the multi-party elections in the territory of Bosanski Samac. Out of the six political parties, three were nationalist or ethnically based. The remaining three political parties were not ethnically based.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Same story, like before, several days. The witness said three parties were national, not nationalistic, and it appears in row -- sorry, it's 21st, page 20 -- page 49, line 21, "nationalist," but we just heard that he said "national parties," which is rather different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please clarify that with the witness, Mr. di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You heard that exchange. The parties that emerged, the HDZ, the SDA, and the SDS, what were they, nationalistic parties or national parties?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: I think that at that stage, when they participated in the elections in 1990, I think that in that context, those parties - we are talking about the Serbian Democratic Party, the Party of Democratic Action, and the Croatian Democratic Union - that at that time and in those circumstances, those were ethnically based parties, not nationalist parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In the early stage of their development, those parties, did they have a common agenda? By that, I don't necessarily mean an agreed agenda but an agenda that included the same objectives.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: It's hard to say whether the -- they had the same agenda in their platforms. I did not read any of the platforms of any of the parties at the time, but it was quite obvious that the three parties represented themselves as parties that wanted to realise the interests of the ethnic group they tried to represent. That's how I would put it. So one represented the Serbian -- the interests of the Serbian, another of the Croatian people, and the third of the Bosniak people. I cannot talk about their platforms because I never read any of their platforms or, rather, manifestos.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you know if they took any position on the continued existence of the Communist Party? If you don't know, just tell us.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: Well, of course, they took a position regarding the party that was in power before -- that is the Communist Party -- and the three parties tried, through the elections that were held in -- at the time, they wanted to take power, and that's what in effect happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. You've mentioned elections at a municipal level. Were there elections at a national level in Bosnia involving these three parties?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: Yes. The elections were held at the level of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in all the municipalities that existed at the time. I think we are talking about 109 municipalities in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: When were those elections held?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN LUKAC
utterances.text: These elections, as far as I can recall, were held in late 1990. I think it was in December.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I want to ask you if you know the defendants in this case, and I'll start with Mr. Simo Zaric. Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if the Prosecution would like to proceed with the identification of the Defence, I would like now to have a short recess of one and a half minutes and the witness will be brought out of the courtroom and then, according to the order of this Trial Chamber, to rearrange the position of the defendants that we have spoke about several days before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. di Fazio, you've heard that. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, I have, and I've no objection to that, and if it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. So -- MR. DI FAZIO: If the Defence want to do that. Before we embark on that exercise, I just point out that I'm now -- and for the purposes of the Chamber and for the purposes of the Defence, I'm going to now turn to this witness' knowledge of the defendants. That may impact on the matter that I raised before the witness was called, namely, my ability to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Okay, before you turn to the identification. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. I just wonder if by eliciting that evidence, evidence of what this witness knows of these defendants and their backgrounds, whether that would be regarded as a controversial area by the defendants and whether or not they would then regard the witnesses, so to speak, off-limits to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
